prompt: make me a story about a red balloon stuck in a tree
reply:
Anu's red balloon 🎈 caught in the mango tree 🌳. It bobbed just above her fingers. A crow landed beside it and stared 🐦.
[CHIPS]Anu climbs up|Anu calls Appa|Anu waits below[/CHIPS]

prompt: tell me a story about a puppy who is scared of thunder
reply:
Boo the puppy hid under the bed ⛈️. The sky went BOOM again. Then a hand reached under with his ball.
[BIG]🐶[/BIG]
[CHIPS]Boo comes out|Boo stays hidden|Boo barks back[/CHIPS]

prompt: what is a fable
reply:
A fable is a short story that teaches 🦊. Usually the animals talk like people 🐢. The lesson lands at the end.
[FACT]Fable comes from fabula, a Latin word for tale.[/FACT]
[CHIPS]Tell me one|Help me write one|Why animals[/CHIPS]

prompt: i want a small story that teaches sharing
reply:
Two mynas found one biscuit. They both pulled, and it snapped in half. Now each bird had a piece 🐦.
[BIG]🍪[/BIG]
[CHIPS]Now a waiting story|Help my own fable|Make it rhyme[/CHIPS]

prompt: does my story need a bad guy
reply:
No 🙂. Trouble is enough on its own. A storm or a locked gate works too 🔒.
[QUIZ]Which one is trouble?[/QUIZ]
[CHIPS]A locked gate|A sunny day[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i tell where my story is happening
reply:
Small details do it 🏠. A sound, a smell, a person. Try a temple bell and frying onions 🔔.
[STEPS]Name one sound|Name one smell|Say who is there[/STEPS]
[CHIPS]Try my beach scene|Sounds for a market|Is mine too plain[/CHIPS]

prompt: my story is only two lines is that ok
reply: Yes ✅. Two lines can be a whole story. Read yours out loud to someone tonight 📖.

prompt: i wrote the first bit of my story can you finish it
reply:
Paste it here and I will read it 📖. Then we build the next bit together. You choose what happens next 🙂.
[CHIPS]Here is my start|Give me one idea|What could go wrong[/CHIPS]

prompt: what should my character want in the story
reply:
What does your character want most? A mango, or a missing shoe. Wanting it makes your story move 👟.
[BIG]🎯[/BIG]
[CHIPS]Mine wants water|Help me pick one|What stops them[/CHIPS]

prompt: make a funny story about a dosa that ran away
reply:
The dosa slid off the plate. It rolled out past a surprised cow 🐄. Behind it came Patti with a ladle 🥄.
[BIG]🫓[/BIG]
[CHIPS]The dosa hides|The cow helps|Patti gives up[/CHIPS]

prompt: my two characters are having a fight what do they say
reply:
Keep the lines short and about one thing 🗨️. Like this. “Give it back.” “It was mine first.” 😮
[CHIPS]They want the ball|Help them make up|One more line[/CHIPS]

prompt: tell me a sleepy story about the moon and an owl
reply:
Here is a small night one 🌙🦉.
[POEM]The owl asked the moon to wait,
the moon just slid on by.
So the owl sat and watched it go
all the way down the sky.[/POEM]
[CHIPS]One more verse|Say it slowly|What happens tomorrow[/CHIPS]

prompt: can an auto rickshaw be a character in my story
reply:
Yes! Give it one habit and a name 😄. Maybe it sneezes every time it starts.
[BIG]🛺[/BIG]
[CHIPS]Name my auto|What does it want|Make it grumpy[/CHIPS]

prompt: write me a short story about a kid who finds an old key in the sofa
reply:
Vikram was digging in the sofa for the remote and came up with a key 🔑 — brass, heavier than it looked, its paper tag worn blank. Nobody in the house admitted to owning it. That night he remembered the storeroom door, and the lock on it that nobody uses 🚪.
[CHIPS]Try the storeroom lock|Ask someone at home|Put it back[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i write a fable with a moral that isn't preachy
reply:
Let the ending do the teaching instead of a closing sentence 🦊. If your greedy crow ends up with an empty beak, the reader works the rest out, and readers enjoy working it out ✂️.
[STEPS]Decide the moral first|Build one event that proves it|Delete the line that states it[/STEPS]
[CHIPS]Check my last line|Try one on me|Morals without stating them[/CHIPS]

prompt: my story characters just walk around and nothing happens
reply:
That usually means nobody wants anything yet 🎯. Give your main character one clear want, then put something solid in the way: she wants the last bus ticket, and her brother is already at the counter. Walking turns into a chase the moment there is a want plus an obstacle 🚧.
[FACT]Plot once meant a small piece of ground.[/FACT]
[CHIPS]Pick my hero's want|Obstacle ideas|Mine still wanders[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i describe a market so readers can smell it
reply: Markets are loud, so pick three details and trust them 🧺. Coriander crushed underfoot, the cold iron smell off a fish tray, someone shouting a price twice. Skip the wide view — a reader builds the whole market out of three sharp things. Next time you are in one, stand still for a minute and collect yours 🐟.

prompt: continue my story where the lights go out during class
reply:
Here is one way in, then it is yours ⚡. The fan slowed to a stop and the whole class made that long ooooh sound. In the dark someone's chair scraped, and Miss Fathima's torch found the classroom door standing open 🔦.
[CHIPS]A cat got in|It was the wind|Voice in the corridor[/CHIPS]

prompt: how long should a short story be
reply:
Long enough to finish the job, and not one scene more 📏. A short story usually holds one problem, one attempt, one change — that is the whole shape. If yours keeps growing it is often two stories stuck together, so pick the one you actually care about ✂️.
[CHIPS]Is mine two stories|Mine feels too long|Where to cut[/CHIPS]

prompt: my villain has no reason for being mean
reply:
Give them a want that makes sense from inside their own head 🎭. Nobody wakes up planning to be the villain — they want the prize, or the last word, or to be believed. Let that want push them one step past fair, and the reader will feel it 🪞.
[QUIZ]Which one is a real motive?[/QUIZ]
[CHIPS]He is just evil|He wants the credit[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i write a story from my dog's point of view
reply:
Cut everything your dog could not know 🐕. No clock times and no reading the label on the tin, but smells arrive first and loudest, and Appa's mood shows up in which shoes he picks. The trick is not doggy talk, it is a narrower window on the same house 🏠.
[CHIPS]Try my cat instead|What a dog notices|Start with a smell[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i end my story without saying it was all a dream
reply:
The dream ending feels like a cheat because it deletes everything the reader just cared about 😴. Aim instead for the moment the change lands: your character wanted something, and now they either have it or have stopped wanting it. One small closing image beats one big explanation 🎬.
[CHIPS]Show me an example|Try a quiet ending|Endings that changed someone[/CHIPS]

prompt: make up a fable about a river and a stone
reply:
The river told the stone to move, and the stone said no. So the river went around, year after year, until one morning the stone found itself sitting in a dry field with no water anywhere 💧. Being stubborn is only useful if you are stubborn about the right thing.
[BIG]🪨[/BIG]
[CHIPS]Give it a title|Write the crow one|Try a kinder ending[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i make a scary story that isn't gory
reply:
Gore is loud, and loud stops being scary fast. What actually unsettles a reader is one small wrong detail in an ordinary place: the gate you definitely latched, standing open 🚪. Keep the thing mostly unseen and the room completely normal, and the reader's own imagination does the work.
[BIG]🕯️[/BIG]
[CHIPS]Try my dark corridor|Wrong detail ideas|How to end it[/CHIPS]

prompt: my dialogue sounds like a robot
reply: Real people interrupt, trail off, and answer a question nobody asked 🗨️. Robot dialogue is everyone speaking in full polite sentences that hand over exactly the right information at exactly the right time. Read your scene aloud tonight to someone at home, and wherever you would never say it that way, break the sentence 🎤.

prompt: i want to write a story set in my grandmother's village
reply:
Places you have actually stood are the easiest to write and the hardest to see, because your eye stopped noticing them years ago 🌾. Walk it in your head, then write only what is doing something 🏡.
[STEPS]Pick one time of day|Note three things moving|Write those, skip the postcard[/STEPS]
[CHIPS]Start at the gate|What to leave out|Help my opening line[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do writers make you care about a character fast
reply:
Sympathy is cheap; investment is what you want 🎯. Two things do most of the work: show the character wanting something specific, and let them be good at one small thing. Wanting creates direction, competence creates respect, and once you respect someone you start worrying about them. Danger alone does nothing, because you cannot fear for a stranger you have no reason to like.
[QUIZ]Which makes a reader care faster?[/QUIZ]
[CHIPS]She is in danger|She wants the scholarship[/CHIPS]

prompt: what makes a fable different from any story with a message
reply:
A fable is built backwards 🦉. The moral comes first and the plot exists only to demonstrate it, which is why fables stay short, the characters are types rather than people, and nothing happens that is not evidence. A novel with a message argues; a fable proves. That constraint is the fun of it, because you get one situation and it has to be airtight.
[CHIPS]Write one with me|Fables that argue back|Types versus characters[/CHIPS]

prompt: my short story has too many characters
reply:
Every named character is a promise you have to keep 📉. If someone appears twice and changes nothing, merge them into a character who is already there, since one person carrying two jobs is more interesting than two people carrying half each. A short story usually survives on a main character, someone who wants the opposite, and maybe one voice from outside. Cut the rest and watch the survivors get room.
[FACT]Protagonist comes from Greek words meaning first actor.[/FACT]
[CHIPS]Which two to merge|List mine and check|Crowd scenes still fine[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i write a scene where two characters disagree
reply:
Give both sides a real argument, including the one you disagree with ⚖️. A scene where a sensible person argues with someone who has no case carries no tension, because the result was decided before anyone spoke. Let them talk past each other for a while, since real arguments are two people answering different questions. Then end it before anyone is convinced, as minds rarely change inside the scene.
[FACT]Argument comes from a Latin word meaning to make clear.[/FACT]
[CHIPS]Both sides sound weak|When to end it|Who should win[/CHIPS]

prompt: is it okay to base a character on someone i actually know
reply:
Writers do it constantly, and the useful version is to borrow the trait, not the person 🪞. Take your uncle's habit of answering a question with a longer question, then hand it to someone with a different age, job, and problem. A real person copied whole comes out flat, because you write what you know about them instead of what the story needs. And nobody agreed to be in your story.
[CHIPS]Traits worth borrowing|Check my character|Telling them or not[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i write an ending that feels earned
reply:
An earned ending uses something the story already planted 🎬. If your character solves it with a skill, a person, or an object we met earlier, the reader feels clever; if help arrives from nowhere they feel cheated and often cannot say why. So read your first half looking for what is already lying around, and let the character choose rather than be rescued.
[QUIZ]Which ending feels earned?[/QUIZ]
[CHIPS]A stranger saves her|Her old trick works[/CHIPS]

prompt: should my story be first person or third person
reply:
Which do you want the reader locked out of? 🔒 First person is intimate and limited: everything arrives through one head, which is ideal for secrets and for a narrator who is wrong about things. Third person can cross the corridor and let us know more than the character does, and that is where dread lives. Try your hardest scene both ways and keep the one that hurts more.
[CHIPS]Try mine both ways|Narrators who are wrong|Present or past tense[/CHIPS]

prompt: my setting is just scenery how do i make it matter
reply:
Scenery sits there; a setting pushes back 🌪️. Make the place cause at least one problem: a power cut during the exam, a bus that comes twice a day, a house where every conversation is overheard. Then give your character a relationship with it, since the same street reads differently to someone leaving and someone stuck. Description is cheap; consequence is not.
[FACT]Scene comes from skene, the tent behind an ancient Greek stage.[/FACT]
[CHIPS]Make mine push back|Weather as obstacle|Too much description[/CHIPS]

prompt: write me a story that ends on a hard choice
reply:
Ten seconds before the district final, Anitha saw that the runner in lane three — the only girl fast enough to beat her — had a lace trailing loose 🏃. Saying nothing would not be cheating, and nobody would ever know she had seen it. Saying something might cost her the one race she had trained two years for. The starter raised his arm.
[CHIPS]Tell her quickly|Say nothing|Point at her shoe[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i keep tension when nothing violent happens
reply:
Tension is an unanswered question with a cost attached ⏳. A conversation where one person knows something the other does not can be unbearable, and nobody raises their voice. Add a clock — the guests arrive at seven, results are read on Friday — and every ordinary sentence starts ticking. Violence is one way to raise stakes and also the laziest, because it ends the question instead of stretching it.
[CHIPS]Add a clock|Quiet scenes with dread|Mine drags in middle[/CHIPS]

prompt: what is subtext in dialogue
reply:
Subtext is the conversation happening under the words 🗨️. Someone asks whether you ate, and means: are you still angry with me. It works because people avoid saying the important thing directly, so the scene stays about the plates while the real argument moves underneath. Write the honest version first, then delete the line that says it out loud and see what survives.
[FACT]Dialogue comes from Greek words for through and speech.[/FACT]
[CHIPS]Test my scene|Lines to delete|When to be direct[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i write a character who is nothing like me
reply:
Start from what they want and why it makes sense to them, not from how different they are 🧭. Difference written from outside turns into a costume: an accent, a hobby, a label, and no interior. Find one thing you genuinely share, being tired of explaining yourself, say, and build outward from there. If you cannot argue their side convincingly, you do not know them well enough yet.
[CHIPS]Interview my character|Research or imagine|Check for costume[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i turn something that really happened to me into a story
reply:
Life supplies material, not structure 🧩. Real events have no shape, because things happen only because Tuesday followed Monday, and the interesting part sits inside an hour of nothing. So take the moment that mattered and invent freely around it: compress three arguments into one, move it somewhere with more pressure, give someone a want they never had. Loyalty to the feeling matters more than loyalty to the facts.
[FACT]Fiction comes from a Latin word meaning to shape.[/FACT]
[CHIPS]Find my real moment|What to invent|Writing about family[/CHIPS]

prompt: my story ideas are always the same shape
reply:
That is usually your favourite question turning up in different costumes, and it is not a flaw, since many writers circle the same few obsessions for a whole career 🔁. What goes stale is the machinery: same age of hero, same problem, same solve. So change one structural thing on purpose. Give the hero the opposite temperament, or start at the ending, or leave the problem unsolved.
[CHIPS]Name my repeated shape|Break one rule|Prompts that force change[/CHIPS]
